quoted_clause: **Scenario:** ~2,000 users, ~5% concurrent (≈100 simultaneous), ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak. ... For 1,000 requests/hour (≈0.28 rps — a light illustrative load ...)
observed: The chapter's own scenario states ~10 rps average, but the routing arithmetic that produces every headline number in the chapter runs at 1,000 requests/hour = 0.28 rps — 36× below the scenario's average load. The "canonical volume" used for the second savings figure (6.24M requests/month) is ≈2.37 rps average, a third value, and 4.2× below the scenario's 10 rps average (10 rps × 2.628M s/mo ≈ 26.3M requests/month). The scenario's stated load is therefore never used to produce any savings, host count, or cost figure in the chapter, and the peak-to-average ratio implied by the scenario (40/10 = 4×) is inconsistent with the canonical volume paired with the same 40-rps peak (40/2.37 ≈ 17×).
correction: Choose one traffic basis for the chapter's worked example and derive everything from it. If the scenario is 10 rps average / 40 rps peak, state the implied monthly volume (≈26.3M requests/month) and recompute the savings at that volume; if the canonical 6.24M/month is to be used, restate the scenario's average as ≈2.4 rps and reconcile the peak-to-average ratio with Ch 17. Keep the 1,000 req/hr figure only as an explicitly labelled unit-normalization illustration, not as the chapter's savings basis.
acceptance_test: Every rate, volume and savings figure in §18.3 is derived from one stated traffic basis, and the chapter states the peak-to-average ratio it assumes.
verdict_evidence: chapter-18/chapter-18.md §4 reads 'To operate a mixed fleet we measure four cross-cutting metrics:' followed by a table with five rows, the fifth being '**Token latency p95 per model (diagnostic)**'; count of body rows = 5 vs stated 4.

quoted_clause: **The mixed fleet needs more hosts than the single-model fleet under the shared placement (58 vs 31 — 27 extra hosts; 39 vs 21 — 18 extra — on the no-derate pair).** ... In our example, consolidation wins because the MoE and 8-bit models capture the same request classes at lower cost, and the FP16 tier handles the tail without contention.
observed: §18.3.3 establishes that the shared-pool mixed fleet requires 18–27 MORE hosts than the single-model fleet, and explicitly says the token-rate saving "must be weighed against *that* placement's extra hosts' amortization and energy: total cost = host amortization + energy + token cost, not token cost alone." §18.5 then asserts, without performing that weighing, that "consolidation wins." Using the book's own only per-host cost figure ($155,817/mo ÷ 21 hosts ≈ $7,420/host/mo average; §18.3.2 basis note), 18 extra hosts ≈ $133,560/mo against a canonical-volume token saving of ≈$69,654/mo (§18.3.3 Volume basis) — i.e. the chapter's own numbers point the other way, and even the marginal (non-staff) host cost plausibly exceeds the saving.
correction: In §18.5, replace the unconditional "consolidation wins" with the conditional result the chapter's own numbers support: the mixed fleet wins on token rate but loses on total cost under the shared placement unless the extra hosts' amortization is offset by higher utilization or a cheaper hardware basis; state the sign explicitly as undetermined until a per-host marginal cost is supplied, and show the break-even (e.g. required marginal host cost ≤ $69,654/18 ≈ $3,870/host/mo). Alternatively, adopt the dedicated placement (20/32 hosts) as the worked example's placement, which is the only one whose host count is at or below the single-model fleet, and say so.
acceptance_test: A reader can state, from §18.5 alone, which placement the chapter adopts, what the total-cost comparison is, and what the verdict is — and the verdict is consistent with §18.3.3's host counts and §18.3.2's per-host cost.
verdict_evidence: §3.3 requires the weighing ('the ~$8,147/month token saving must be weighed against *that* placement's extra hosts' amortization and energy: total cost = host amortization + energy + token cost, not token cost alone. The sign of the host delta is a placement decision') and reports 58 vs 31 / 39 vs 21 hosts, yet §3.5 concludes 'In our example, consolidation wins because the MoE and 8-bit models capture the same request classes at lower cost' with no host-cost figure; at ch18's own basis (~$155,817/21 ≈ $7,420/host/mo) 18 extra hosts ≈ $133.6K/mo against the ~$69,654/mo canonical-volume token saving.
fix_instruction: Qualify §3.5: state that consolidation wins on token rate but, under the adopted shared placement, the 18–27 extra hosts' amortization+energy (≈$134–200K/mo at the Ch 16 per-host basis) exceeds the ≈$69.7K/mo saving, so the total-cost sign is undetermined until a marginal per-host cost is supplied (break-even ≈ $69,654/18 ≈ $3,870/host/mo); or adopt the dedicated placement (20/32 hosts) as the worked example's placement and say so.

quoted_clause: A chat UI tolerates ~200 ms of added service latency per request ... Acceptable for interactive chat (typical threshold: ≤500 ms). ... **Consolidate** when: workload profile overlap ≥70%, latency tolerance ≥300 ms, and cost differential >30%. ... the latency criterion is met against the ≤500 ms interactive threshold of §18.3.4, not the ~200 ms chat tolerance quoted in §18.2 — L̄ ≈ 247 ms clears 500 ms and exceeds 200 ms
observed: The chapter carries two different interactive-chat latency budgets (200 ms in §18.2, 500 ms in §18.3.4) and the consolidation verdict depends on which one applies. Worse, the consolidation criterion is written in terms of the workload's *tolerance* ("latency tolerance ≥300 ms") but is checked against the *achieved* weighted latency (L̄ ≈ 247 ms). Under the criterion as written, the scenario's tolerance is either 200 ms (fails) or 500 ms (passes); under the check as performed, 247 ms fails a 300 ms criterion. The referent note therefore does not actually establish that the criterion is met.
correction: Rewrite the criterion to be about the workload's declared budget, e.g. "latency budget ≥300 ms per request (the deployment's SLO, not the achieved latency)", and state the scenario's budget once, in one place, as 500 ms (the §18.3.4 interactive threshold), removing the 200 ms figure from §18.2 or explicitly marking it as a different quantity (e.g. added service latency above a baseline). Then check the criterion against the declared budget and state the achieved L̄ separately.
acceptance_test: The chapter contains one interactive latency budget, used consistently in §18.2, §18.3.4 and §18.5; the consolidation criterion is stated in terms of the same quantity it is checked against.
verdict_evidence: ch18 L126 'consolidation wins because the MoE and 8-bit models capture the same request classes at lower cost' conflicts with the 70/20/10 split in §18.3.3 (L91-93), where 8-bit serves routine requests and MoE serves high-quality-reasoning requests — different classes.
fix_instruction: Rewrite as '…because the 8-bit and MoE tiers together capture ~90% of request classes at lower cost than FP16' (or add the comparator 'the classes the FP16 tier would otherwise absorb').

quoted_clause: spreading that cost across a mixed fleet improves effective cost/token
observed: The phrasing 'spreading that cost across a mixed fleet' is misleading. The FP16 model's cost is not spread across the mixed fleet — it is borne by the FP16 tier and the requests routed to it. The mixed fleet improves overall cost/token by routing most traffic to cheaper models, not by distributing the FP16 cost across all tiers.
correction: Rewrite to: 'routing most traffic to cheaper models while reserving FP16 for the tail improves effective cost/token' or 'amortizing the FP16 host cost over the requests that actually need FP16, rather than running every request on FP16, improves effective cost/token.'
acceptance_test: A reader does not infer that the FP16 cost is distributed across all tiers of the mixed fleet.
verdict_evidence: §18.3.1 says the co-resident tiers are ~350 GB, "leaving ~290 GB for KV cache", then three sentences later uses "640 − 350 − 64 = 226 GB" ("the pool's KV falls to ~226 GB and C to ~9"); 290 omits the 64 GB runtime reserve that the table row above states.
fix_instruction: Replace with "That is ~350 GB of weights, leaving ~290 GB before the ~64 GB runtime/workspace reserve — ~226 GB for KV (the figure used below: C = ⌊226/24.89⌋ = 9)".

The general principle (qualify before promoting) is relevant, but the Intel-specific details (three footnotes about Intel hardware and OpenVINO documentation) dominate the subsection and feel like they belong in a deployment/qualification chapter. The text acknowledges 'This is a general qualification procedure illustrated with an Intel example, not a claim about the mini-case's AMD Ryzen node,' but the Intel details still dominate.

verdict_evidence: "that same 20/32 group is at or slightly below the single-model fleet's 21/31" — 20 < 21 but 32 > 31, so the policy pair is slightly above, not below.

page_hint: §18.3.1, co-residency bullet list vs the paragraph immediately following it
quoted_clause: Two 70B 4-bit GGUF (≈70 GB total; ... and hold no canonical KV reservation, so the sole-resident 436 GB KV assumption of the table above still governs the active tiers) ... **290 GB < the canonical 436 GB KV budget, so the FP16 tier cannot co-reside at the canonical profile.** KV, not weights, is the binding term: as the FP16 row above notes, that tier's KV alone is the canonical 436 GB; with the §18.3.1 co-resident weights (~350 GB) the pool's KV falls to ~226 GB and C to ~9

Both cannot be true. The 436 GB figure is the FP16-tier-alone budget (640 − 140 − 64) and is void once the 8-bit, MoE-8-bit and 4-bit weights are resident. The bullet's clause is the one that survives into the reader's memory and it is the wrong one.
correction: Delete the clause "so the sole-resident 436 GB KV assumption of the table above still governs the active tiers" and replace it with the co-resident figure: "the pool's KV budget under this configuration is 640 − 350 − 64 = 226 GB, i.e. C = 9 concurrent canonical requests (§18.3.3)". Also fix the sentence "the FP16 tier cannot co-reside at the canonical profile" — the FP16 tier IS co-resident in this list; what cannot happen is co-residing at the canonical KV profile.
acceptance_test: The chapter contains exactly one KV budget for the co-resident configuration (226 GB) and one for the FP16-alone configuration (436 GB), each attached to the configuration it describes.
verdict_evidence: ch18 L68 states the two 4-bit copies 'hold no canonical KV reservation, so the sole-resident 436 GB KV assumption of the table above still governs the active tiers'; L70 immediately states 'with the §18.3.1 co-resident weights (~350 GB) the pool's KV falls to ~226 GB and C to ~9'. Both cannot be true of the same pool.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the L68 clause to: the 4-bit copies reserve no KV, but they do consume ~70 GB of weights, so the 436 GB sole-resident figure is void under co-residency; the governing budget is the ~226 GB / C = 9 computed below. Keep 436 GB only as the FP16-tier-alone reference.

quoted_clause: Under the **dedicated** placement the ledger reverses: that same 20/32 group is at or slightly below the single-model fleet's 21/31.
observed: The comparison is stated as "at or slightly below", but the policy pair is 32 vs 31 — above, not below — and the no-policy pair is 20 vs 21 — below. The sentence collapses two different comparisons into one directional claim, and the direction it asserts for the policy case is wrong.
correction: Rewrite: "Under the dedicated placement the ledger roughly balances: 20 hosts vs 21 for the single-model fleet without the utilization derate, and 32 vs 31 with it — the mixed fleet's advantage is at most one host, not a reduction."
acceptance_test: No directional comparison in §18.3.3 or §18.5 states a sign that the printed numbers do not support.
verdict_evidence: ch18 L105: dedicated is '20 hosts / 32 with policy', single-model is '21/31'. 20 vs 21 is below but 32 vs 31 is above, so 'that same 20/32 group is at or slightly below the single-model fleet's 21/31' is false for the policy pair.
fix_instruction: Replace with: 'under dedicated placement the no-policy pair falls below the single-model fleet (20 vs 21) while the policy pair is marginally above it (32 vs 31) — the ledger narrows rather than reverses.'

quoted_clause: **Ignoring capital amortization.** FP16 on 8×H100 has high upfront cost; spreading that cost across a mixed fleet improves effective cost/token. Don't forget to annualize GPU capex in the per-token math.
observed: The claimed benefit is contradicted by the chapter's own arithmetic: the mixed fleet under the shared placement needs 18–27 more hosts (§18.3.3), so total capital amortization rises, not falls. Spreading a fixed cost over a fleet improves effective cost/token only if the fleet raises utilization of the same capital; the chapter's placement arithmetic shows the opposite. As written, a reader could take away "mixing models lowers capital cost per token" as a general rule.
correction: Rewrite the correction to the actual mechanism: "amortizing capex over tokens requires utilization, not model diversity. A mixed fleet lowers the token rate only if it raises the utilization of the same installed capital; if it requires additional hosts (as in §18.3.3), total cost per token can rise even as the nominal rate falls."
acceptance_test: No claim in §18.5 asserts a cost benefit that §18.3.3's host arithmetic contradicts.
verdict_evidence: ch18 L150 says 'spreading that cost across a mixed fleet improves effective cost/token', while L105 shows the shared placement needs 27 more hosts (58 vs 31), so total capex amortization rises; the entry's own heading ('Ignoring capital amortization') does not support the 'spread it across a mixed fleet' advice.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the entry: 'Ignoring capital amortization. FP16 on 8xH100 carries high upfront cost; annualize GPU capex into the per-token rate and compare placements at the same volume. A mixed fleet does not by itself reduce capital per token — under the shared placement of §18.3.3 it adds 18–27 hosts; it lowers cost per token only where the added hosts raise utilization of capacity that would otherwise sit idle.'

quoted_clause: N_tail = ⌈λ_tail·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ = ⌈4 × 8.6/(17 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈34.4/11.305⌉ ≈ **4 hosts** at the canonical 40-rps peak.
observed: Two problems. (a) u and ρ are never defined in the chapter, and the same product 0.665 is decomposed differently in §18.3.3, where it is called "the 70%×95% policy" (routing mix × quality pass rate) rather than utilization × ρ. A reader cannot tell whether 0.70 is a utilization factor or the routine-traffic share. (b) The formula uses C = 17, the single-model canonical concurrency, while the chapter's own mixed shared-pool configuration has C = 9 (§18.3.1/§18.3.3); the tail tier (FP16) in the mixed fleet therefore has a different per-host capacity than the formula assumes. The arithmetic itself (34.4/11.305 = 3.04 → 4) is correct.
correction: Define u and ρ explicitly (e.g. u = target utilization, ρ = policy/quality derate) and use the same decomposition as §18.3.3; state which C applies ("C = 17 for a dedicated FP16 tier; C = 9 for the shared pool of §18.3.3") and give the resulting host count for each.
acceptance_test: Every symbol in the N_tail formula is defined in the chapter, and the C used is the C of the configuration the chapter actually adopts.
verdict_evidence: ch18 L151 uses N_tail = ⌈λ_tail·W/(C·u·ρ)⌉ with u and ρ never defined anywhere in the chapter (grep for 'utilization' returns only L83/L105 prose), while the same product 0.665 is called 'the 70%×95% policy' at L105; C = 17 is the single-model canonical concurrency whereas the chapter's adopted shared pool has C = 9 (L105). Arithmetic itself checks out: 4×8.6 = 34.4, 17×0.70×0.95 = 11.305, 34.4/11.305 = 3.04 → 4.
fix_instruction: Define the symbols inline ('u = utilization target 0.70, ρ = policy yield 0.95') or replace u·ρ with the chapter's existing '70%×95% policy' label, and state whether C = 17 (single-model) or C = 9 (shared mixed pool) applies to the tail tier's hosts.

quoted_clause: target the **fleet-weighted average** under the §18.3.2 per-1M basis (e.g. fleet-weighted average < $2.50/1M — not the FP16 tier's own rate, which is itself $2.50/1M) for competitive SaaS [ASSUMPTION — benchmark claim unsourced]

verdict_evidence: ch18 L136: 'fleet-weighted average < $2.50/1M — not the FP16 tier's own rate, which is itself $2.50/1M' — the target and the excluded quantity are the same number, so the parenthetical refutes itself; the mixed fleet's own blend is ~$1.33/1M, so the stated target is cleared by construction.
fix_instruction: Replace with a target that is not identical to the FP16 row: e.g. 'fleet-weighted average below the FP16 tier's $2.50/1M rate — the §18.3.3 blend is ~$1.33/1M, so the metric tracks drift away from the dominated single-tier configuration rather than a tight budget.'

page_hint: Fig 18.1 caption and surrounding text (§18.8 end)

quoted_clause: **Treating quantization as free.** 4-bit/8-bit models reduce VRAM but increase CPU cycles and may lower quality on long-context tasks.
observed: The stated cost of quantization is CPU cycles, which is the mechanism for CPU/GGUF execution, not for GPU-resident 8-bit weights. The chapter's own 8-bit tier runs on H100s (§18.3.1, §18.8 Tier 2), where the cost of 8-bit is dequantization overhead and reduced Tensor Core efficiency at that precision, plus a possible KV-format change — not CPU cycles. As written, the mistake entry teaches the wrong mechanism for the chapter's dominant tier.
correction: Split the mechanism by execution device: "quantization is not free: on CPU/GGUF it adds dequantization work per token (and the §18.3.4 arithmetic shows why the CPU tier cannot meet an interactive SLO); on GPU it reduces weight memory and can raise effective latency at reduced-precision Tensor Core throughput, and it may lower quality on long contexts."
acceptance_test: Each quantization claim in §18.5 names the execution device whose behavior it describes.
verdict_evidence: ch18 L148 says '4-bit/8-bit models reduce VRAM but increase CPU cycles', yet the 8-bit tiers run on H100s (L52 '2 (70 GB weights + 24.9 GB FP16 KV ...)'; L81 '70B dense 8-bit on 2×H100'; L186 Tier 2 '1×H100'), where the quantization cost is dequant/reduced-precision Tensor Core throughput, not CPU cycles.
